newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish financial markets welcome labour reforms.
newsitem.headline: Spanish financial markets welcome labour reforms.

text.p: The Spanish labour reform package announced on Wednesday should further hearten financial markets but the impact is expected to be muted as the measures had been expected.

The package, announced on Wednesday after months of intense negotiations, is designed to reduce Europe's highest unemployment rate of just under 22 percent and liberalise one of the continent's most rigid labour markets.
The cornerstone of the deal is the reduction in the cost of shedding labour, which should help reduce upward price pressure.
"Financial market reaction to the labour market deal will be favourable because it should go some way to moderating labour costs," said Craig Shute, fixed-income analyst at Bear Stearns.

Under the new permanent contract, employers will be required to pay unfair dismissal costs of only 33 days per year worked, rather than the current 45, with a maximum of 24 months, instead of 42 months.
"The impact (of the package) will be minor. The effect on the markets will be moderately optimistic," said Antonio Villarroya, an economist with Merrill Lynch in Madrid.
Spanish financial markets have been climbing swiftly since the beginning of April, benefiting from an optimistic domestic economic outlook that the reform pact helps underscore.
The IBEX-35 index of leading shares has risen five percent since April 3, while the June 10-year bond future contract has risen 3.6 points since April 2.
"We've viewed this generally as a small step moving in the right direction and we're encouraged," said Donald Smith, international economist at HSBC in London.
"Coupled with an impressive performance on inflation and the fiscal deficit this will support market confidence," he said.
Markets expect inflation to moderate further, which could prompt the Bank of Spain to modestly reduce its official interest rate of 5.75 percent as soon as April 15.

March inflation, due on Friday, is seen moderating to 2.4 percent or less from 2.5 percent in February -- the lowest level in 28 years. Inflation has been cut by nearly half from 3.9 percent in January 1996.
